objectives: Trace metallurgy from the Bronze and Iron Ages through the Bessemer revolution and the birth of metallography.
Read the iron-carbon phase diagram and identify austenite, ferrite, cementite, and pearlite.
Locate and interpret the eutectoid point at 0.76 wt% C and 727 degrees C.

slides.title: From the Bronze Age to Bessemer: a history of metals
slides.body:
**Metallurgy** is the science and craft of extracting metals from their ores and shaping their properties. Its history is the history of civilization itself. The **Bronze Age** (roughly 3300-1200 BCE) began when smiths in Mesopotamia and Anatolia learned to alloy **copper** with about 10% **tin**, producing **bronze** — far harder than either parent metal. Bronze tools and weapons gave their owners decisive advantages, and the recipe spread across Eurasia.

The **Iron Age** (from roughly 1200 BCE) arrived when smiths in Anatolia, likely among the **Hittites**, mastered the higher temperatures and reducing conditions needed to win iron from its oxides. Early **wrought iron** was soft, but smiths discovered that heating iron in a charcoal fire absorbed **carbon** at the surface, producing **steel** that could be hardened by quenching. **Damascus steel** and the Japanese **tatara** furnace producing **tamahagane** for katana blades are famous expressions of this empirical art.

For millennia, metallurgy advanced by trial and tradition rather than theory. The decisive industrial leap came in **1856**, when the English engineer **Henry Bessemer** patented the **Bessemer process**: blowing air through molten **pig iron** to burn off excess carbon and silicon, converting brittle cast iron into steel in minutes rather than days. Bessemer's converter, refined by **Robert Forester Mushet** with the addition of **spiegeleisen** (a manganese-rich alloy) to control oxygen and sulfur, slashed the price of steel and enabled railroads, skyscrapers, and bridges. The competing **Siemens-Martin open-hearth process**, developed by **William Siemens** and **Pierre-Emile Martin**, soon followed and dominated bulk steelmaking into the twentieth century.

This lesson begins our study of the single most important diagram in ferrous metallurgy. The visualization here is the **iron-carbon phase diagram**, the map that tells a metallurgist which crystalline phases exist at any combination of carbon content and temperature.

slides.title: The birth of metallography: Sorby and Roberts-Austen
slides.body:
Understanding *why* steel behaves as it does required seeing its internal structure. That breakthrough came from the English geologist and microscopist **Henry Clifton Sorby** (1826-1908). Around **1863**, Sorby adapted techniques he had developed for examining thin sections of rock and applied them to polished, chemically etched samples of iron and steel. Viewing them under a reflected-light microscope, he revealed for the first time that steel is not homogeneous but is built from distinct **microconstituents** with characteristic shapes. Sorby is rightly called the **father of metallography** — the study of the microstructure of metals.

Sorby identified the laminated, fingerprint-like constituent later named **pearlite** for its mother-of-pearl iridescence under the microscope. His work showed that the **mechanical properties** of a steel — its hardness, strength, and toughness — are governed by the *arrangement* of its phases, not merely by overall composition. This insight founded the entire discipline of **physical metallurgy**.

The quantitative phase diagram that organizes these observations owes much to **Sir William Chandler Roberts-Austen** (1843-1902), chemist and metallurgist of the **Royal Mint** in London. Using the newly invented **thermocouple** and his own recording **pyrometer**, Roberts-Austen measured the temperatures at which iron-carbon alloys change phase, and around **1897-1900** he published the first systematic **iron-carbon equilibrium diagram**. In his honor, the high-temperature solid solution of carbon in face-centered-cubic iron was named **austenite**.

The theoretical foundation for all such diagrams is the **phase rule** of the American physicist **Josiah Willard Gibbs**, published in his 1876-1878 treatise *On the Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Substances*. The Gibbs phase rule, $F = C - P + 2$, relates the number of degrees of **freedom** $F$ to the number of **components** $C$ and **phases** $P$. The Dutch chemist **Hendrik Willem Bakhuis Roozeboom** applied Gibbs's thermodynamics to construct rigorous phase diagrams in the 1890s, turning Sorby's pictures and Roberts-Austen's measurements into a predictive science. Together these workers transformed metallurgy from craft into engineering.

slides.title: Reading the iron-carbon diagram: phases and the eutectoid
slides.body:
The **iron-carbon phase diagram** plots temperature against carbon content (in weight percent, wt% C). Steels contain up to about **2.1 wt% C**; above that, up to roughly 6.7 wt% C (the composition of pure cementite), the alloys are **cast irons**. The diagram identifies several key solid phases.

- **Austenite** (gamma-iron, $\gamma$): a solid solution of carbon in **face-centered cubic (FCC)** iron, stable at high temperature. Its open FCC interstices dissolve up to about **2.1 wt% C** at 1147 degrees C. Named for Roberts-Austen.
- **Ferrite** (alpha-iron, $\alpha$): a solid solution of carbon in **body-centered cubic (BCC)** iron, stable below 912 degrees C. Ferrite is soft and ductile and dissolves very little carbon — a maximum of only about **0.022 wt% C** at 727 degrees C.
- **Cementite** (iron carbide, $Fe_3C$): a hard, brittle **intermetallic compound** containing 6.67 wt% C. It is metastable but persists indefinitely in ordinary steels.
- **Pearlite**: not a phase but a **lamellar microconstituent** — alternating thin plates of ferrite and cementite — formed when austenite of eutectoid composition decomposes on cooling.

The heart of the steel region is the **eutectoid point**, located at **0.76 wt% C and 727 degrees C** (older texts often quote 0.8% C / 723 C). At this point a single solid phase transforms on cooling into two solid phases simultaneously:

$$\gamma\,(0.76\%\,C) \rightarrow \alpha\,(0.022\%\,C) + Fe_3C\,(6.67\%\,C)$$

This **eutectoid reaction** produces pearlite. Steels are classified by where they sit relative to this point. A **eutectoid steel** has exactly 0.76% C and transforms entirely to pearlite. A **hypoeutectoid steel** (below 0.76% C) first precipitates **proeutectoid ferrite** along grain boundaries, then the remaining austenite becomes pearlite. A **hypereutectoid steel** (above 0.76% C) first forms **proeutectoid cementite**, then pearlite. The boundary lines have classical names: the **A1 line** at 727 degrees C is the eutectoid (lower-critical) temperature; the **A3 line** marks the onset of ferrite formation in hypoeutectoid steels; and the **Acm line** marks cementite formation in hypereutectoid steels. The maximum-carbon eutectic of cast iron — austenite plus cementite, called **ledeburite** — sits at 4.3 wt% C and 1147 degrees C. Mastering this map lets a metallurgist predict the microstructure, and therefore the properties, of any plain-carbon steel from its composition and thermal history alone.

question.question: On the iron-carbon diagram, the eutectoid reaction occurs at approximately which composition and temperature?
question.explanation: The eutectoid point sits at 0.76 wt% C and 727 degrees C. There, austenite decomposes into ferrite plus cementite, forming pearlite. The 4.3% C / 1147 C point is the eutectic (ledeburite); 2.1% C marks the maximum carbon solubility in austenite; 6.67% C is the composition of pure cementite.

hints: The eutectoid is the all-solid reaction in the steel range, not the cast-iron eutectic.
It is the lowest point of the austenite region in the steel portion of the diagram.
slides.workedSolution: The eutectoid invariant point is defined at 0.76 wt% C and 727 degrees C (option B). At this single point, gamma austenite transforms isothermally into alpha ferrite (0.022% C) plus cementite Fe3C (6.67% C), generating the lamellar microconstituent pearlite. The other options correspond to the eutectic, the austenite carbon-solubility limit, and the carbide composition respectively.

question.question: Classifying a steel from its carbon content
question.prompt: You receive a plain-carbon steel rail reported to contain 0.45 wt% carbon, and you slowly cool a sample from 950 degrees C (fully austenitic) to room temperature. Using the iron-carbon diagram, explain whether this is a hypoeutectoid, eutectoid, or hypereutectoid steel. Describe the sequence of phases that appear as the sample crosses the A3 line and then the A1 line at 727 degrees C, and predict qualitatively the final room-temperature microstructure in terms of proeutectoid ferrite and pearlite.

question.question: Cementite has the formula Fe3C. Using atomic masses Fe = 55.85 and C = 12.01 g/mol, compute the carbon content of pure cementite in weight percent, to one decimal place.
question.hint: Mass of carbon = 12.01. Mass of Fe3C = 3(55.85) + 12.01 = 179.56. Weight percent C = 12.01 / 179.56 times 100 = 6.7%.

question.question: Who pioneered metallography by applying reflected-light microscopy to polished and etched steel around 1863, revealing its microconstituents for the first time?
question.explanation: Henry Clifton Sorby, a geologist skilled in preparing thin sections of rock, adapted those methods to metals around 1863 and is regarded as the father of metallography. Bessemer revolutionized steel production; Gibbs founded the thermodynamics of phase equilibria; Roberts-Austen produced the first systematic iron-carbon diagram and lent his name to austenite.

hints: He was a geologist before he was a metallurgist.
His name is not attached to a phase; another worker's is.
slides.workedSolution: Henry Clifton Sorby (option C) brought petrographic microscopy to metals, polishing and etching steel and observing constituents such as pearlite under reflected light. This founded metallography. Roberts-Austen later quantified the iron-carbon diagram and is honored in the name austenite; Bessemer and Gibbs contributed to production and to phase-rule thermodynamics respectively.

question.question: Why the Bessemer process changed the world
question.prompt: Before 1856, converting brittle high-carbon pig iron into usable steel was slow and costly. Explain in metallurgical terms what Henry Bessemer's converter actually accomplished by blowing air through molten pig iron, why Robert Mushet's addition of manganese-rich spiegeleisen was necessary, and how lowering the carbon content moves an alloy leftward across the iron-carbon diagram from the cast-iron range toward the steel range. Comment on why cheap steel was transformative for railroads and construction.
